questions.stem: Radioactivity was first discovered in 1896 in uranium salts by:
questions.explanation: Becquerel noticed that uranium salts fogged a photographic plate in the dark — invisible emissions. He shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with Marie and Pierre Curie. Marie Curie coined the term 'radioactivity' and later isolated polonium and radium. Rutherford identified the three types of radioactivity (alpha, beta, gamma) and later the nucleus (1911 gold-foil experiment).

questions.stem: Which type of radioactive radiation has the highest penetrating power?
questions.explanation: Gamma rays — massless, no charge, electromagnetic waves of very short wavelength — pass through paper, aluminium, even centimetres of lead. Need dense shielding (thick lead / concrete). Alpha (helium-4 nucleus) — stopped by a sheet of paper or a few cm of air. Beta (electron / positron) — stopped by a few mm of aluminium. Ionising power inverts — alpha > beta > gamma.

questions.stem: The 'half-life' of a radioactive isotope is the time needed for:

options.option_text: Half of the atoms to decay

questions.explanation: Half-life (T₁/₂) — time for the number of radioactive nuclei to fall to half their original value. After 2 half-lives, 1/4 remains; after 3, 1/8. Half-lives span many orders of magnitude — Uranium-238: 4.5 billion years (age of the Earth); Carbon-14: 5,730 years (used for dating organic remains); Iodine-131: 8 days (used in thyroid scans). Activity follows the same exponential decay as the nuclei.

questions.stem: In nuclear FISSION, energy is released when:

options.option_text: A heavy nucleus splits into lighter ones
A gas condenses to a liquid

questions.explanation: Fission — a heavy nucleus (e.g., Uranium-235) absorbs a slow neutron and splits into two smaller nuclei + more neutrons + energy. The energy comes from mass-defect — the products weigh slightly less than the reactants; the missing mass is released as energy via E = mc². A single fission of U-235 releases ~200 MeV. Self-sustaining chain reactions power reactors and (uncontrolled) atom bombs. Fusion combines light nuclei (e.g., H → He in the Sun).

questions.stem: Nuclear FUSION — the process that powers the Sun — requires:
questions.explanation: Fusion needs temperatures of ~15 million K (Sun's core) or ~100-200 million K (in an experimental reactor like ITER) so nuclei have enough kinetic energy to overcome their Coulomb repulsion and get close enough for the strong nuclear force to bind them. Magnetic confinement (tokamaks, stellarators) and inertial confinement (laser implosion) are the two main experimental approaches on Earth. ITER (France, under construction) is the world's largest fusion project.

questions.stem: The radioactive isotope used for carbon dating of archaeological samples is:
questions.explanation: C-14 — produced continuously in the upper atmosphere by cosmic rays; absorbed by plants (CO₂) and then animals. After death, no new C-14 is added, and the existing C-14 decays with a half-life of 5,730 years. Measuring the ratio C-14 / C-12 gives the age of organic remains. Useful up to ~50,000 years (7 half-lives; after that, too little C-14 remains to measure). Potassium-argon dating is used for much older (volcanic) rock.

questions.stem: India's first nuclear reactor, commissioned in 1956 at Trombay, was:
questions.explanation: APSARA — India's first research reactor — built at BARC, Trombay (Mumbai) in 1956, inaugurated by Jawaharlal Nehru. 1 MW thermal, swimming-pool type. Homi J. Bhabha led the Indian atomic programme. Cirus (40 MW, 1960, Canadian-supplied) came next. Dhruva — a larger research reactor (100 MW, 1985) — built indigenously. Tarapur-1, 2 (1969) were India's first commercial power reactors, built with US collaboration.
